\chapter{Past Five, and the Balance Turns Over}
\label{ch:gu-six-to-ten}
\hlchaptermodality{43}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can count from one to ten in Gujarati, write the one new letter that eight needs, and build the ordinal of any number from seven upward without ever being taught the word.}

Complete GU-R39-one-to-ten: run ek to das without stopping, then run the ordinals and say which five of the ten you built rather than learned.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[chha]{\gu{છ} (chha) — six, and a shape you have been writing since chapter two}

\label{lesson:GU-C39-chha}



\begin{quote}
The last chapter ended on a condition. This one answers it, so the recalls come first.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} run \textbf{\gu{પહેલું}} to \textbf{\gu{પાંચમું}} in order — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{third}, and what it kept of \textbf{\gu{ત્રણ}} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say a \textbf{\gu{જો} … \gu{તો} …} condition — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\gu{જો}} the count goes past five, \textbf{\gu{તો}} the balance of built and received ordinals turns over. That was the promise. This chapter is the \textbf{\gu{તો}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \gu{છ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{છ}} — \emph{chha} — \textbf{six}
\end{quote}

One letter. No sign attached, no second letter behind it — the whole number is a single consonant carrying its own inherent \emph{a}.

And it is not a new letter. You have been writing \textbf{\gu{છ}} since chapter two, inside \textbf{\gu{છે}} and \textbf{\gu{છું}}. What is new is that the shape can stand on its own and mean a quantity.

\textbf{\gu{એક}, \gu{બે}, \gu{ત્રણ}, \gu{ચાર}, \gu{પાંચ}, \gu{છ}.}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: one shape, two entries}]
Wiktionary does not give \textbf{\gu{છ}} one entry. It gives it two, side by side, and they have nothing to do with each other:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{entry} & \textbf{what it says} \\
\midrule
the letter & \emph{the seventh consonant in Gujarati} \\
the numeral & \emph{six} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So the sign that sits \textbf{seventh} in the alphabet is the word for \textbf{six}. Two numbers on one shape, and no relation between them at all. Say the word, not the position.

Behind it: Middle and Old Gujarati \emph{cha}, Prakrit \emph{cha}, Sanskrit \emph{ṣáṣ}. A word worn down to one letter over that whole road.

\textbf{\gu{છ}} is also the last name on a list you already have. \textbf{-\gu{મું}} builds the ordinal of every Gujarati number except \textbf{\gu{એક}}, \textbf{\gu{બે}}, \textbf{\gu{ત્રણ}}, \textbf{\gu{ચાર}} — and \textbf{\gu{છ}}. The previous chapter could name that fifth exception but could not print it, because you had no word for six. Now you do.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ek, be, traṇ, chār, pā̃ch, chha}
  \item \textbf{\gu{છ}} on its own, then read \textbf{\gu{છે}} — same shape, different job
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many letters are in the Gujarati word for six? (\textbf{One.}) Where have you written that letter before? (\textbf{In \gu{છે} and \gu{છું}, since chapter two.}) Which list does \textbf{\gu{છ}} complete? (\textbf{The numbers -\gu{મું} does not build on.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%9B}{Wiktionary: \gu{છ}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/-\%E0\%AA\%AE\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: -\gu{મું}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sāt]{\gu{સાત} (sāt) — seven, and the place the balance turns}

\label{lesson:GU-C39-saat}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{six}, and name the one letter it is — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{second}, and the shape it shares with \emph{third} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\gu{જો}} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\gu{જો}} is two signs. \textbf{\gu{સાત}} is three, and you own all three: \textbf{\gu{સ}}, the attached \textbf{\gu{ા}}, and \textbf{\gu{ત}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \gu{સાત}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{સાત}} — \emph{sāt} — \textbf{seven}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\gu{એક}, \gu{બે}, \gu{ત્રણ}, \gu{ચાર}, \gu{પાંચ}, \gu{છ}, \gu{સાત}.}

This is the first number past the exception list, and that changes what a number is worth to you. \textbf{-\gu{મું}} does not build on \textbf{\gu{છ}}. It does build on \textbf{\gu{સાત}}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{સાતમું}} — \emph{sātmũ} — \textbf{seventh}
\end{quote}

You were not taught that word. You assembled it, out of a number you learned thirty seconds ago and an ending you have had for five lessons. \textbf{\gu{બીજું}} and \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}} could not be assembled from anything; they had to be handed to you whole. From here up, they do not.

\begin{cousinweb}
Wiktionary hands \textbf{\gu{સાત}} down from Prakrit \emph{satta}, and that from Sanskrit \emph{saptá}.

Watch the middle of the word: \emph{pt} $\to$ \emph{tt} $\to$ \emph{t}. The cluster does not simplify in one step; it first becomes a doubled consonant, and only then thins to a single one. That is exactly the road chapter twelve walked for \textbf{\gu{બે}} — \emph{dv} $\to$ \emph{bb} $\to$ \emph{b}.

And the word did not simply shrink. Where Sanskrit had a short \emph{a} before two consonants, Gujarati has a long \textbf{\gu{ા}} before one. The syllable kept its weight and paid for the lost consonant with a longer vowel.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chha, sāt} — then read \textbf{\gu{સાત}} sign by sign
  \item \emph{saptá, satta, sāt} — the cluster thinning, the vowel lengthening
  \item \emph{bījũ}, then \emph{sātmũ} — received, then built
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{seventh}, and where did you get it? (\textbf{\gu{સાતમું}} — \textbf{built from \gu{સાત} and -\gu{મું}}.) Which earlier number took the same three-step road? (\textbf{\gu{બે}}: \emph{dv} $\to$ \emph{bb} $\to$ \emph{b}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%B8\%E0\%AA\%BE\%E0\%AA\%A4}{Wiktionary: \gu{સાત}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭha]{\gu{ઠ} — retroflex ttha}

\label{lesson:GU-W22-ttha}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{seven} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{fourth}, and the letter it ends on — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\gu{જ્યારે}} and use it to locate one event against another — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
\end{itemize}

Six and seven cost you no new sign at all. \textbf{\gu{જ્યારે}} the count reaches eight, that stops — so the sign is bought here, one lesson before the number needs it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the square you already hold three corners of}
Gujarati keeps two rows of \emph{t}. One is dental — tongue at the teeth. One is retroflex — tongue curled back. Each row has a plain letter and a breathy one.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{plain} & \textbf{aspirated} \\
\midrule
dental & \textbf{\gu{ત}} \emph{ta} & \textbf{\gu{થ}} \emph{tha} \\
retroflex & \textbf{\gu{ટ}} \emph{ṭa} & ? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\gu{ચોથું}} ends on \textbf{\gu{થ}}, the dental aspirate. You have three of the four. The missing corner is the retroflex aspirate, and it is the one the word for eight needs.

\subsection*{Script — meet one form}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{ઠ}} — \emph{ṭha}
\end{quote}

Keep \textbf{\gu{ઠ}} visible. Start high, a little to the right of where the ring will sit. Curl left across the top and down the outside of a small hook. From the foot of the hook, sweep down and to the right until you reach the widest point on the right. Now carry the ring round \textbf{clockwise} — down the right side, along the bottom, up the left — and close it exactly where your diagonal crossed on the way down. One stroke, no lift.

\textbf{\gu{ટ}} turns the other way. Its bowl runs anticlockwise and finishes still open on the right; \textbf{\gu{ઠ}} runs clockwise and finishes closed. If the ring will not close, you have made a \textbf{\gu{ટ}}.

\subsection*{Writing — notice and trace}
Finger-trace \textbf{\gu{ઠ}} once, then air-trace it once. Notice the hook, the diagonal into the ring, and the closing point.

\subsection*{Writing — copy with the model}
Copy visible \textbf{\gu{ઠ}} once. Compare only two things: does the ring close, and does it close where the diagonal came in? Repair one landmark if needed.

\subsection*{Writing — recall after hiding}
Hide the model and write retroflex \emph{ṭha} once. Uncover \textbf{\gu{ઠ}}, compare, and stop after one repair.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\gu{ટ} \gu{ઠ} \gu{થ}} aloud and keep all three apart. Which of the four corners is still missing from the two \emph{t} rows? (\textbf{None} — with \textbf{\gu{ઠ}} the square is complete.)

Sources: \href{https://www.t30apps.com/gujarati-alphabet-writing/}{Gujarati Alphabet Writing Practice} and the \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0A80.pdf}{Unicode Gujarati chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āṭh]{\gu{આઠ} (āṭh) — eight, and a number that loses nothing}

\label{lesson:GU-C39-aath}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\gu{ઠ}} from memory — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{first}, and what Prakrit put where Sanskrit had an \emph{m} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} build a \textbf{\gu{જો} … \gu{તો} …} condition and score yourself on it — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \gu{આઠ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{આઠ}} — \emph{āṭh} — \textbf{eight}
\end{quote}

Two signs: the independent \textbf{\gu{આ}} you have had since chapter one, and the \textbf{\gu{ઠ}} you made yourself last lesson. Nothing else.

\textbf{\gu{એક}, \gu{બે}, \gu{ત્રણ}, \gu{ચાર}, \gu{પાંચ}, \gu{છ}, \gu{સાત}, \gu{આઠ}.}

\begin{cousinweb}
Wiktionary hands \textbf{\gu{આઠ}} down from Prakrit \emph{aṭṭha}, and that from Sanskrit \emph{aṣṭá}.

Set it beside last lesson's word:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Sanskrit} & \textbf{Prakrit} & \textbf{Gujarati} \\
\midrule
\emph{saptá} & \emph{satta} & \textbf{\gu{સાત}} \\
\emph{aṣṭá} & \emph{aṭṭha} & \textbf{\gu{આઠ}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two numbers, one road, and the same three steps every time: a cluster of two different consonants, then a doubled consonant, then a single one with a long vowel standing in front of it. Seven and eight did not each have a history. They had the same history.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: a number that keeps everything}]
\textbf{\gu{આઠમું}} — \emph{āṭhmũ} — \textbf{eighth}. Built, like \textbf{\gu{સાતમું}}, and again from nothing you had to be told.

Hold that against \textbf{\gu{પહેલું}}. \emph{First} keeps not one sound of \textbf{\gu{એક}}; its \textbf{\gu{લ}} stands where Sanskrit \emph{prathama} had an \emph{m}, and the number vanished on the way. \textbf{\gu{આઠમું}} keeps \textbf{\gu{આઠ}} entire. The top of your count and the bottom of it behave in opposite ways, and now you can see both at once.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chha, sāt, āṭh} — then count from \textbf{\gu{એક}}
  \item \emph{pahelũ}, then \emph{āṭhmũ} — nothing kept, everything kept
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two of your numbers came down the same three-step road? (\textbf{\gu{સાત}} and \textbf{\gu{આઠ}}.) What is \emph{eighth}? (\textbf{\gu{આઠમું}}.) Which ordinal keeps nothing of its number at all? (\textbf{\gu{પહેલું}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%86\%E0\%AA\%A0}{Wiktionary: \gu{આઠ}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nav]{\gu{નવ} (nav) — nine, and the number that came through whole}

\label{lesson:GU-C39-nav}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{eight}, and name its two signs — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\gu{તે}}, and say who it is for — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\gu{તે}} points at somebody who is not in the room. In a moment you will be able to point at the ninth of anything, which is a different kind of pointing and needs a number first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \gu{નવ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{નવ}} — \emph{nav} — \textbf{nine}
\end{quote}

Two consonants, no attached sign at all: \textbf{\gu{ન}} carrying its inherent \emph{a}, then \textbf{\gu{વ}}. Both have been in your hand since the first two chapters.

\textbf{\gu{એક}, \gu{બે}, \gu{ત્રણ}, \gu{ચાર}, \gu{પાંચ}, \gu{છ}, \gu{સાત}, \gu{આઠ}, \gu{નવ}.}

\begin{cousinweb}
Wiktionary hands \textbf{\gu{નવ}} down from Sauraseni Prakrit \emph{nava}, and that from Sanskrit \emph{náva}.

Read that line twice. Nothing happened. Sanskrit \emph{n}, Gujarati \textbf{\gu{ન}}; Sanskrit \emph{v}, Gujarati \textbf{\gu{વ}}; only the last vowel fell away, which is what happens to every Gujarati word.

Now look back over the chapter:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{what it lost} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\gu{છ}} & a whole second syllable — \emph{ṣáṣ} to one letter \\
\textbf{\gu{સાત}} & the \emph{p} of \emph{saptá} \\
\textbf{\gu{આઠ}} & the \emph{ṣ} of \emph{aṣṭá} \\
\textbf{\gu{નવ}} & nothing \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four numbers, and only one of them arrives with every consonant still standing.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chha, sāt, āṭh, nav}
  \item \emph{náva}, then \emph{nav} — and hear how little moved
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which number in this chapter reaches Gujarati with every consonant intact? (\textbf{\gu{નવ}}.) Which one lost the most? (\textbf{\gu{છ}} — a whole syllable.) What is \emph{ninth}? (\textbf{\gu{નવમું}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%A8\%E0\%AA\%B5}{Wiktionary: \gu{નવ}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[das]{\gu{દસ} (das) — ten, and one word with two spellings}

\label{lesson:GU-C39-das}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nine} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say both words for \emph{we}, and say which one shuts the listener out — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
\end{itemize}

Hold those two words. The last number of the chapter is about to make a group you might or might not be standing inside.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \gu{દસ}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{દસ}} — \emph{das} — \textbf{ten}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\gu{દ}} then \textbf{\gu{સ}}. Two consonants, no signs, nothing new.

\textbf{\gu{એક}, \gu{બે}, \gu{ત્રણ}, \gu{ચાર}, \gu{પાંચ}, \gu{છ}, \gu{સાત}, \gu{આઠ}, \gu{નવ}, \gu{દસ}.}

Ten words, and the count is closed at last.

\begin{cousinweb}
Wiktionary hands \textbf{\gu{દસ}} down from Sauraseni Prakrit \emph{dasa}, and that from Sanskrit \emph{dáśa}. Sanskrit's \emph{ś} — the sound of \textbf{\gu{શ}} — arrives in Gujarati as plain \textbf{\gu{સ}}.

Then the entry adds one more line, and it is the interesting one: \textbf{\gu{દસ}} is a \textbf{doublet} of \textbf{\gu{દશ}}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{spelling} & \textbf{said} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\gu{દસ}} & \emph{das} \\
\textbf{\gu{દશ}} & \emph{daś} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One Sanskrit word, two Gujarati words, both alive. The everyday one wore the sibilant down; the other kept the \textbf{\gu{શ}} the Sanskrit had. You have held both letters for a long time, so you can read either without being told which is which — and that is worth knowing before you meet the second one printed somewhere.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\gu{અમે}}, then \textbf{\gu{આપણે}}, then \emph{das} — and say which of the two words would put you inside a group of ten
  \item \emph{das}, then \emph{dasmũ}
  \item \textbf{\gu{દસ}}, then \textbf{\gu{દશ}} — same number, two spellings
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Count to ten. What is the other spelling of \emph{ten}, and what does it keep? (\textbf{\gu{દશ}} — the \textbf{\gu{શ}} of Sanskrit \emph{dáśa}.) What is \emph{tenth}? (\textbf{\gu{દસમું}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%A6\%E0\%AA\%B8}{Wiktionary: \gu{દસ}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sātmũ · āṭhmũ · navmũ · dasmũ]{Where the rule starts, and where it stops}

\label{lesson:GU-C39-ordinal-reach}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ten}, and its other spelling — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\gu{તે}} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
\end{itemize}

Keep \textbf{\gu{તે}} on the page. It ends this lesson inside a sentence nobody taught you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the list has two edges}
Wiktionary's entry for \textbf{-\gu{મું}} says it forms the ordinal of every Gujarati number \emph{but} \textbf{\gu{એક}}, \textbf{\gu{બે}}, \textbf{\gu{ત્રણ}}, \textbf{\gu{ચાર}}, \textbf{\gu{છ}}.

You now hold all five of those words — and, for the first time, the numbers on the \emph{other} side of them. So the list stops being a list and becomes a \textbf{boundary}, with an edge at each end:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{edge} & \textbf{what it says} \\
\midrule
the bottom edge & \textbf{\gu{પાંચ}} is \emph{not} on the list: \textbf{\gu{પાંચમું}}. \\
the exceptions & \textbf{\gu{એક}}, \textbf{\gu{બે}}, \textbf{\gu{ત્રણ}}, \textbf{\gu{ચાર}}, \textbf{\gu{છ}} — five, each learned whole. \\
the top edge & \textbf{\gu{છ}} is the last name on it. From \textbf{\gu{સાત}} up, \textbf{-\gu{મું}} every time. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\gu{છ}} is the interesting edge, because it sits \emph{inside} the count: the rule works at five, stops at six, starts again at seven. Wiktionary gives the sixth as \textbf{\gu{છઠ્ઠું}}, on a doubled \textbf{\gu{ઠ}}. This book does not ask you to use that word — only to see that the exception is real, and is not the number with \textbf{-\gu{મું}} behind it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built: four ordinals nobody taught you}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{number} & \textbf{ordinal} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\gu{સાત}} & \textbf{\gu{સાતમું}} \\
\textbf{\gu{આઠ}} & \textbf{\gu{આઠમું}} \\
\textbf{\gu{નવ}} & \textbf{\gu{નવમું}} \\
\textbf{\gu{દસ}} & \textbf{\gu{દસમું}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four words, no new lesson, no new sign — and it does not stop at ten.

Wiktionary's own example for the suffix is \textbf{\gu{દસમો} \gu{મહિનો}}, \emph{the tenth month}, masculine because \textbf{\gu{મહિનો}} is. Put \textbf{\gu{તે}} in front and the sentence finishes itself:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{તે} \gu{દસમો} \gu{મહિનો} \gu{છે}.} — \emph{te dasmo mahino chhe} — \textbf{It is the tenth month.}
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sātmũ, āṭhmũ, navmũ, dasmũ}
  \item the five words the rule refuses
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the exception list stop? (\textbf{At \gu{છ}}.) What happens above it? (\textbf{-\gu{મું}}, every time.) How many new words did this lesson teach? (\textbf{None.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/-\%E0\%AA\%AE\%E0\%AB\%81\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: -\gu{મું}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%9B}{Wiktionary: \gu{છ}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{One to ten, and the promise kept}

\label{lesson:GU-R39-one-to-ten}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, then the run.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} name both edges of the exception list — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{six}, and the one letter it is — \textbf{R2}, seven lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\gu{જે}}, the word for \emph{the one that} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\gu{ભાત}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\gu{ભાત}} and \textbf{\gu{સાત}} end in the same two signs, so a new number rhymes with an old word. \textbf{\gu{જે}} and an ordinal work from two sides: \textbf{\gu{જે}} names \emph{the one that}, \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}} names \emph{which one}. Nothing new arrives here.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the ten numbers in order, then backwards from \textbf{\gu{દસ}}
  \item \textbf{\gu{જે}} \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}} \gu{છે} — \emph{the one that is third}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter, in one number}]
The last chapter finished on a condition: \textbf{\gu{જો}} this book took the count past five, \textbf{\gu{તો}} the balance of built and received ordinals would turn over. Here is what it turned into.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{received whole} & \textbf{built with \textbf{-\gu{મું}}} \\
\midrule
first to fifth & \textbf{\gu{પહેલું} \gu{બીજું} \gu{ત્રીજું} \gu{ચોથું}} & \textbf{\gu{પાંચમું}} \\
sixth to tenth & the sixth, left to the dictionary & \textbf{\gu{સાતમું} \gu{આઠમું} \gu{નવમું} \gu{દસમું}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One-in-five became four-in-five. \textbf{\gu{બીજું}} and \textbf{\gu{ત્રીજું}} still share their \textbf{-\gu{ીજું}}, and \textbf{\gu{પહેલું}} still keeps nothing of \textbf{\gu{એક}} — but those are facts about the bottom of the count, not about Gujarati. Above the list the language adds an ending and never stops.

The whole chapter cost \textbf{one letter}: only \textbf{\gu{આઠ}} needed a new sign, and that was \textbf{\gu{ઠ}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How far can you count? (\textbf{To \gu{દસ}}.) How many of the ten ordinals can you build unaided? (\textbf{Five} — the fifth, and the seventh to the tenth.) Which letter did this chapter buy? (\textbf{\gu{ઠ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
